Original Article
Echoing Intelligence: Assessing the Capabilities of a Novel
Generative AI With a Large Language Model in Cardiology
Education
Muneeb Ahmed, MD,a Flora Huang, MD, FRCPC,b and
Chi-Ming Chow, MD, MSc, FRCPC, FCCS, FASEa
a
Department of Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada
b
North York General Hospital, Toronto, Ontario, Canada
ABSTRACT
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) holds promise for enhancing
medical education, particularly in complex fields like cardiology. We
assessed the ability of a large language model (LLM) to generate and
evaluate educational material comparable to that created by human
experts.
Methods: We trained an AI model on cardiology-specific content using
80 lectures from the St. Michael’s Hospital Virtual Echo Rounds. The AI
generated 10 multiple-choice questions (MCQs), and experienced
cardiologists crafted an additional 10 MCQs. Eleven postgraduate year
4-6 cardiology trainees answered all 20 questions and attempted to
identify the source (AI or human) of each question. The AI also
answered the same set of questions. We analyzed performance using
the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and recognition ability.
Results: Trainees scored similarly on AI-generated and humangenerated questions (median 8/10 vs 8/10; P > 0.05). Their ability
to identify the source of questions did not exceed chance levels (median correct identifications: 10/20; P > 0.05). The AI achieved 95%
accuracy on AI-generated questions and 100% on human-generated
questions.
Conclusions: The AI-generated educational content was of comparable quality to that produced by human experts, and trainees could not
reliably distinguish between the 2 sources. Our findings suggest that AI
could significantly augment cardiology education by providing highquality, scalable learning resources.

Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have opened
new avenues for enhancing medical education. In cardiologyda field characterized by rapidly expanding
knowledge and complex clinical scenariosdthere is a
pressing need for innovative educational tools that can
adapt to individual learning needs. Traditional educational
methods may struggle to keep pace with the evolving

Previous studies have demonstrated AI’s capacity to
personalize educational material and improve learner engagement. Wartman and Combs1 emphasized the transition from
information dissemination to intelligent, adaptive learning
systems in medical education. Masters underscored the practical framework AI provides, facilitating critical thinking and
application.2 Moreover, Narayanan et al.3 highlighted AI’s
ability to address individual knowledge gaps and offer realtime feedback, enhancing learning outcomes. Cheung et al.4
found that AI-generated examination questions matched the

quality of those created by human experts, even in high-stakes
settings like medical licensing examinations. Additionally,
Chan and Zary5 discussed how AI tutors could revolutionize
medical education by providing personalized learning experiences. Liu et al.6 explored the role of AI in medical education,
highlighting its potential to transform traditional teaching
methods.
Canadian-specific educational frameworks and guidelines
have also evolved to reflect the need for innovation. The Royal
College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada emphasizes
competency-based medical education, and the Canadian
Cardiovascular Society (CCS) provides nationally recognized
guidelines and standards for training and practice.7,8 AI-based
educational tools may align with these principles by supporting learners as they progress toward milestones and
competencies laid out by these Canadian bodies. Such tools
could strengthen adherence to Canadian guidelines in areas
like heart failure management, valvular disease, and imaging
protocols and ensure consistent, high-quality instruction
across diverse training sites in Canada.
Building on this foundation, our study aimed to evaluate
the effectiveness of a large language model (LLM) in generating and assessing cardiology educational content. By
comparing trainee performance on AI-generated vs humangenerated questions and assessing their ability to distinguish
between them, we sought to understand AI’s potential role in
advancing cardiology education.
Methods
Study design
We conducted an exploratory study involving 11 cardiology trainees from a Canadian universityeaffiliated training
program. Participation was voluntary, and all participants
provided informed consent privately. We conducted the study
in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Formal institutional ethics approval was not obtained, as
the study was considered an educational quality improvement
initiative that did not involve sensitive personal data or interventions affecting patient care.
Data source and AI training
We used the Podcast AI platform to transcribe 80 publicly
available echo rounds (St. Michael’s Hospital Virtual Echo
Rounds) for their comprehensive coverage of echocardiographic and cardiovascular topics.7 A research assistant
manually reviewed these transcripts for major errors to ensure
accuracy of medical terminology. We trained a GPT-4ebased
LLM on these verified transcripts. The LLM restricted itself
from having real-time access to the Internet or external databases during question generation; it operated on a closed

data set. We used reinforcement learning techniques to optimize question quality based on relevance, difficulty, and
alignment with educational objectives.
Participants
Eleven participants in this study were postgraduate year 4-
6 cardiology trainees in a Canadian universityeaffiliated
program. They had each regularly attended echocardiography
teaching sessions. Inclusion criteria included cardiology
training program enrollment and informed consent provision.
We aimed for a pilot, all-comers approach. Because the total
available trainees rotating through echocardiography during
the time of our study was 11, we included all volunteers for a
sample of convenience. This approach, typical of preliminary
feasibility studies, allowed us to gauge the viability of AIgenerated questions and compare them to expert-generated
questions without a formal power calculation.
Intervention
We administered 20 multiple-choice questionsd10
generated by our LLM AI and 10 crafted by experienced
cardiologists. Trainees answered all 20 questions and
attempted to identify whether each question was generated by
the AI or by a human. The specific AI-generated and humangenerated questions are available in Supplemental Table S1.
Outcomes
The primary outcomes were as follows:
 Trainee performance on AI-generated vs humangenerated questions
 Trainees’ ability to correctly identify the source of
each question
Secondary outcomes included the AI’s performance on
both sets of questions.
Statistical analysis
We compared individual trainee scores for AI-generated
and human-generated questions using the Wilcoxon signedrank test, which is appropriate for paired, nonparametric
data. We chose this test because of the small sample size and
the non-normal distribution of score differences. The test
assumes that differences between paired observations are
symmetrically distributed around the median.
For the Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing trainee
scores, n represents the number of nonzero differences (in this
case, n ¼ 8 trainees with nonzero differences). We calculated
the exact P value to determine statistical significance.
We assessed trainees’ ability to recognize the source of
questions using the same test, comparing their recognition
rates against a chance level of 50%, here, n ¼ 8 trainees with
nonzero differences from chance recognition rates. We set
statistical significance at P <0.05. We performed analyses

using R, version 4.0.3 (R Foundation for Statistical
Computing, Vienna, Austria).

Results
Trainee performance
Trainees achieved a median (interquartile range [IQR]) score
of 8 (7-9) out of 10 on the AI-generated questions and 8 (7-8) out
of 10 on the human-generated questions (Tables 1 and 2). The
Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed no significant difference between the 2 sets of scores (T ¼ 13; n ¼ 8; P ¼ 0.65), indicating
comparable performance. Trainees correctly identified the
question source (AI vs human) only 51.4% of the time (median
[IQR], 10 [8-12] of 20), which did not exceed chance levels (T ¼
18; n ¼ 9; P ¼ 0.68; Table 3). Our analysis revealed no significant bias toward overcalling questions as either AI-generated or
human-generated (50% of AI questions overcalled as human and
47% of human questions overcalled as AI).
AI performance
The AI achieved the following:
 Accuracy on AI-generated questions: 95% (9 of 10
correct)
 Accuracy on human-generated questions: 100% (10
of 10 correct)
 Correct identification of question source: 55% (11 of
20)
Discussion
Our findings demonstrate that an AI model can generate
high-quality educational content for cardiology trainees,
yielding scores comparable to those obtained from humangenerated questions. Although we included only 11 participants, this pilot sample provided preliminary evidence that
AI-generated questions can effectively assess knowledge and
clinical reasoning in complex medical domains. These results
align with previous work such as Cheung et al.,4 who reported
that AI-generated examination questions matched the quality
of those created by human experts.
The inability of trainees to distinguish between AI-generated
and human-generated questions highlights the sophistication of
the AI’s language and content generation capabilities. This
finding suggests that AI-generated content can be seamlessly
integrated into existing educational frameworks without
compromising the authenticity of learning materials. Similarly,

Hashimoto et al. 8 discussed how AI systems could generate
clinically relevant content that meets educational standards.
Our results have particular relevance in the Canadian
context. As cardiology training programs nationwide aim to
maintain high standards of teaching, AI-driven educational
tools could provide a uniform baseline of complexity and
content quality, regardless of geographic location or institutional resources. By aligning AI-generated content with Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines and the Royal
College’s competency-based frameworks, educators can ensure
trainees receive consistent instruction that reflects national
priorities in cardiovascular health care.
The AI’s high performance in answering both AI-generated
and human-generated questions underscores its robust
comprehension of cardiology concepts. This dual capability
suggests potential applications beyond content generation,
such as serving as an intelligent tutor providing immediate
feedback and personalized learning pathways. By leveraging
AI’s adaptability, educators can tailor educational experiences
to individual trainee needs, potentially enhancing learning
efficiency and outcomes.5
Implications for medical education
Integrating AI into medical education could address several
challenges. AI enhances scalability by efficiently generating
extensive educational content, alleviating some of the burdens
on educators. Through adaptive learning algorithms, AI achieves personalization by tailoring material to individual trainee
strengths and weaknesses.6 AI improves consistency in
educational content, ensuring uniform quality and difficulty
across different cohorts.
In the Canadian setting, this consistency extends to
aligning educational content with national standards. The
Canadian health care environment, with its diverse patient
populations and wide geographic distribution of trainees,
could benefit from AI tools that deliver standardized,
guideline-based educational content. This approach ensures
that all Canadian trainees, whether in large urban centers or

cardiology education.
By incorporating AI-generated content, educators may
focus more on mentoring and direct clinical teaching, areas
where human expertise is irreplaceable. This balance could
enrich the educational environment, combining the efficiency
of AI with the nuanced guidance of experienced clinicians.
Limitations
Our study has limitations that warrant consideration. We
conducted this as a feasibility study with a relatively small
sample (n ¼ 11), which may limit generalizability. Larger,
multicenter studies are needed to confirm these results and
explore potential variability across different training programs.
Additionally, we restricted our scope to multiple-choice
questions derived from echocardiography lectures; expanding
question formats to include open-ended cases or clinical
simulations could offer further insight into the AI’s versatility.
Lastly, although we followed up on short-term learning outcomes, we did not assess long-term knowledge retention or
the application of AI-generated content in real-world clinical
decision makingdkey areas for future research.
Future directions
Future research should explore the integration of AIgenerated content into the broader Canadian medical curriculum, including other training programs and specialties.
Assessing the impact of these tools on training standards set by

Canadian governing bodiesdsuch as the Royal Collegedand
evaluating how well they align with CCS guidelines could
further inform the development of AI-driven educational
platforms across the country.
Conclusions
Our AI model demonstrated the ability to generate highquality educational content indistinguishable from that of
human experts. Trainees performed similarly on AI-generated
and human-generated questions and could not reliably identify the source of the questions. These findings support
integrating AI into cardiology education as a tool for augmenting traditional teaching methods and meeting the
evolving needs of learners. Embracing AI’s potential may
contribute to more efficient, personalized, and scalable medical education, ultimately enhancing patient care.
